When reporters ask if he shot the president, Oswald denies it. He tells them, “I’m just a patsy” saying someone set him up to take the blame.

That same night, Jack Rubinstein, a Jewish nightclub owner, is already outside Dallas police headquarters, just feet from Oswald. He tells the FBI he had a pistol. Under oath, his story changes: he says he lied about the gun.

Saturday night, a call goes from Ruby’s sister’s apartment to a restaurant owned by his business partner, Ralph Paul. 

Paul says he’d already left. 
A waitress contradicts him. 
She recalls Paul taking Ruby’s call and asking, “Are you crazy? A gun?” Was that the order?

Just before midnight, Ruby speaks for two minutes with his Jewish friend Breck Wall in Galveston, then calls Paul again from another line. Wall says it was union business. Early investigators suspected someone passed Ruby an order.

At 11:17 a.m., Ruby wires $25 through Western Union. His receipt shows exactly how a payment could carry a coded message. The form reads, “Deliver the following message with the money.”

The FBI never released neither recipient and the message.

At 11:21 a.m., he steps out of the crowd inside police headquarters and shoots Oswald on live TV. Oswald dies before he can tell a jury why he called himself a patsy.
